sources.headline: 'Not again': Arrest of US marine for murder reignites protests in Japan's Okinawa
sources.text: For many Okinawa locals, the arrest of a US soldier accused of robbing and killing a woman in a hotel room has reignited decades of frustration over crimes involving US military personnel there."Honestly my first reaction was, 'Not again,'" 52-year-old longtime Okinawa resident Ai Sato told the BBC."Nothing has changed since I was a child. How many times are we going to repeat the same thing, create more victims, cause their families to suffer, and ultimately, cause the people of Okinawa to grieve?"Akemi Oshiro, a 62-year-old Ginowan resident shared similar sentiments."I know we shouldn't get used to terrible things like this, but because they keep happening, I've stopped being surprised," she told the BBC.Okinawa hosts the largest US military presence in Japan. It is home to several US military bases and tens of thousands of American troops.US Marine Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, was arrested by Japanese police on Sunday. Police say an investigation is underway and that Ballard is in Japanese custody because the alleged crime was unrelated to official military duties.Whether a US service member is acting in the performance of official duty, external or not can determine which country has primary jurisdiction. When Japan has jurisdiction, but the suspect is under US custody, they can retain custody until Japan brings charges.Ballard was assigned to III Marine Expeditionary Force and stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Ginowan City.The Okinawa prefectural police say 39-year-old Anna Yagi was found dead early 3 October in a hotel room in Naha.Security footage allegedly shows a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone with her belongings. Local media citing police have reported that Yagi appeared to have been strangled with a cord.Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi registered an official protest with Washington. But residents like Sato feel that's far from enough."I am deeply disappointed by the same kinds of government comments we have been hearing for decades -- that they will protest or that they take the matter seriously.""I want Prime Minister Takaichi to call President Trump directly, someone with whom she has been emphasizing as having a close relationship with, and discuss concrete measures to prevent this from happening yet again," she said.Following news of the suspected murder, people in Japan have been voicing anger with some 100 people protesting in both Naha and Tokyo. Others took to social media expressing their outrage and demanding justice with one user saying: "Enough is enough."Over the past few years, a number of accidents and crimes have led to growing local opposition to the US presence on the island.The 2016 rape and murder of a 20-year-old local woman saw tens of thousands of protesters demonstrate against the heavy US presence there. A former US marine subsequently received a life sentence for the crime. The US currently has about 55,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, with the heaviest concentration based on the tropical island prefecture. Okinawa is one of the country's smallest prefectures by size, but 70% of the land used exclusively by the US military in Japan is located there.In 1972, Okinawa prefecture was returned to Japanese control after United States forces occupied the islands at the end of the Second World War. Since then, there have been 6,409 arrests for criminal offenses related to US military personnel, according to Okinawa Prefectural Government.Locals say the significant US presence has stirred resentment over a number of issues from crimes including rapes, assaults, and drunk-driving accidents to local disturbances such as noise and aircraft crashes.In 1995, three US servicemen abducted, beat, and raped a 12-year-old schoolgirl as she walked home from a stationery store.In 2025, a US Marine was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a Japanese woman."Even 80 yeas after the war, Okinawa where we live is a place that is so unnerving," 48-year-old mother of two boys Hitomi Miyagi told the BBC."We will not stop raising our voices hoping for an Okinawa, where we can live in peace."

sources.headline: US marine arrested in Japan on suspicion of killing woman, police say
sources.text: A US marine stationed on Japan’s southern island of Okinawa is accused of murdering a Japanese woman and has been arrested on suspicion of murder, police said on Sunday.The suspect allegedly “killed [a] 39-year-old woman at a hotel in Naha and stole her wallet” as well as her backpack, local police told news media outlets.Citing police, NBC News reported that the suspect charged in the case was identified as Lance Cpl Devin Jacob Ballard, 20. Anna Yagi was identified as the victim.Ballard denied the allegations, police said, according to NBC.Crimes including rape, assault, hit-and-run and drunk driving by US personnel have long sparked protests on Okinawa. The island bears a disproportionate burden of hosting about 70% of US military facilities in Japan.US ambassador George Glass posted on social media that he had spoken with Japan’s foreign ministry and Okinawa’s governor, offering “sincere condolences to the victim’s family” and pledging cooperation into the investigation of her death.The Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, said Japan had lodged a protest with US authorities and called the crime “exceptionally brutal and vicious”.The government has urged the US “to provide maximum cooperation with the investigation, enforce stricter discipline among US military personnel, and take thorough measures to prevent the recurrence of similar crimes”, Takaichi said.Public broadcaster NHK and other Japanese media outlets, citing investigation sources, reported that CCTV footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.Police then found a 20-year-old man who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage and asked him to accompany them voluntarily to a local police station, where he was arrested, NHK reported.“We have lost a family member and are deeply saddened,” Yagi’s brother said through local police, according to the Asahi Shimbun daily newspaper. “My parents, in particular, are utterly devastated at the loss of their daughter.”The US has about 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa.Crimes committed by US personnel in Japan have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies.“Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen,” Japan’s defense minister Shinjiro Koizumi said.In June 2025, a Japanese court sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton – then 22 – to seven years in prison after being convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.Earlier, in 2017, former US marine and civilian military base worker Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.The same year, US forces in Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated American marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.According to the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper, about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since Okinawa was returned to Japan from the US in 1972 after the second world war.The number of arrests in a year hit 80 in 2024, the highest in 20 years.

sources.headline: U.S. Marine suspected in woman's death arrested in Japan
sources.text:
U.S. Marine suspected in woman's death arrested in Japan
Transcript
Download
Embed
<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5990879/nx-s1-9951961" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Transcript
A U.S. Marine has been arrested on suspicion of murder in Okinawa, prompting renewed Japanese criticism of the conduct of American military personnel.
Transcript
MICHEL MARTIN, HOST: Japanese authorities have arrested a U.S. Marine on the island of Okinawa. He's suspected of robbing and murdering a local woman. Here's NPR's Anthony Kuhn.ANTHONY KUHN, BYLINE: Japanese media quote Okinawan police as saying a 20-year-old Marine was seen entering a hotel with a 39-year-old local woman, then exiting alone. The woman was later found dead, apparently strangled to death. The Marine is also suspected of taking her wallet and backpack, but he denies the charges, police said. Okinawa Governor Genta Koja spoke to reporters about the case.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)GENTA KOJA: (Through interpreter) It has dealt a massive shock to the people at the prefecture and sparked fresh anxiety. It is absolutely unforgivable, and I feel deeply outraged.KUHN: Japan's foreign minister summoned U.S. Ambassador George Glass to complain. In a social media post, Glass said that he offered condolences and that the U.S. is cooperating with Japanese authorities. Okinawan media have reported that protests have taken place in three cities in Okinawa. Similar actions are planned for Tokyo as well. Governor Koja said that the recurrence of such incidents shows that U.S. military efforts to maintain discipline and educate its personnel have been ineffective.Governor Koja has been in office for less than a week. He won gubernatorial elections last month by focusing on the economy, rather than the U.S. military base issue. Okinawan native Nitsuki Karimata is active in Okinawan civil society. She creates peace studies programs for Japanese schools. She says Okinawans are on the same page about crime by U.S. military personnel.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)NITSUKI KARIMATA: (Through interpreter) While we do have different views on the existence of these bases, we still have to live next to them in Okinawa. But not a single person, whether they oppose or support them, is willing to accept the harm caused by these bases.KUHN: Anthony Kuhn, NPR News.(SOUNDBITE OF BROCKER WAY'S "CHURCH AND STATE")

sources.headline: US marine arrested on suspicion of killing woman in Japan
Japanese leader calls woman's murder, allegedly by U.S. Marine, "heinous crime"
sources.text:
Updated on: October 5, 2026 / 9:53 AM EDT
/ CBS/AFP
Add CBS News on Google
A woman's murder allegedly committed by a U.S. Marine in Okinawa is a "heinous crime," Japan's premier said on Monday, as the new accusation of violence involving American forces sparked public outrage. Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run and drunk-driving incidents by U.S. personnel have long sparked protests on the island, which bears a disproportionate burden of hosting about 70% of U.S. military facilities in Japan. The new case involves Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old U.S. Marine stationed at Futenma Air Station in Okinawa, who was arrested on suspicion of killing 39-year-old Anna Yagi at a hotel in the island's capital city of Naha early Saturday and stealing her wallet and backpack. He has denied the allegations, according to Japanese media.Public broadcaster NHK and other Japanese media outlets, citing investigation sources, reported that CCTV footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.A patrolling police officer then found a 20-year-old man, later identified as Ballard, who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage in an entertainment district in Okinawa City, about 15 miles northeast of Naha. The officer asked him to accompany them voluntarily to a local police station, where he was arrested, NHK reported.His shaved head and the tattoos on his arms matched those of the man in security footage, Kyodo news agency reported.
Devin Jacob Ballard, a U.S. Marine who has been in custody in an alleged robbery and murder of a woman on Japan's southern island of Okinawa, is sent over to the Naha prosecutors' office in Japan on Oct. 5, 2026.
Kotaro Ueda/Kyodo News via AP
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told lawmakers the government has lodged a strong protest with the United States, urging its "full cooperation with the investigation" and "strict discipline among U.S. military personnel.""The occurrence of such a heinous crime is extremely regrettable," Takaichi said.Emotions run highAround 100 people participated in a rally in Naha on Sunday, holding up placards stating their "strong protest" against the murder, Japanese media reported.
Okinawa native Sorane Sakihama, 24, who organized a similar rally in Tokyo on Sunday, said she cried upon learning about the woman's death. "We couldn't protect her. That made me so angry and sad," the university student told AFP, adding that she was planning to organize another protest in front of the U.S. Embassy for Tuesday evening. "I want to ask them — what are these soldiers stationed here for? They might say they are here to protect lives or boost security. But how can they say that when a life was taken by their own?" Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told reporters on Monday that "the government will work with the United States to thoroughly make sure there will be no recurrence, and reduce burdens on local residents."
News of the Marine's arrest immediately prompted Japan's foreign affairs and defense ministers to summon senior U.S. officials to convey their "extreme disappointment" and "lodge strong protests," Kihara said. The incident came just a few weeks after Okinawa elected Genta Koja as its new governor, ending the eight-year rule of his predecessor, who had long pushed for a major U.S. military base to be moved off the island. Koja, 42, accepts a central government plan to keep the U.S. Marine Corps' Futenma air base on Okinawa's main island, but to move it to a less populated location. Calling the murder-robbery "extremely malicious in nature," Koja told reporters on Sunday it had "hugely shocked residents here who are forced to live side-by-side with the bases, and instilled new fear in them."
Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja, right, hands a letter of protest to U.S. Marine Corps Lt. Gen. Benjamin T. Watson at the Okinawa prefectural office in Naha, Okinawa, on Oct. 5, 2026, after Japanese police arrested a U.S. Marine accused of robbing and killing a woman.
Kotaro Ueda / Kyodo News via AP
"I am infuriated," Koja said. He said the incident showed U.S. efforts to "educate soldiers and improve their behavior have not been functioning at all."Koja said he will travel to Tokyo "soon" to lodge a protest with top government officials, including Takaichi.
On Monday, U.S. Ambassador to Japan George Glass said on social media that he is telling U.S. military commanders this week they need "to hold our American service members to the very highest levels of discipline and integrity." He also said that he and Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, discussed the "next steps in strengthening that bond of trust with our Japanese partners and base-hosting communities."Okinawa was under U.S. occupation from World War II until 1972. Today it hosts 70% of America's military facilities and most of the 50,000 U.S. troops based in Japan.There has been anger over increasing crime linked to the U.S. military on the island. The number of U.S. military-related criminal cases rose to 101 last year from about 40 in 2020, according to prefectural police. A Japanese court sentenced a U.S. Marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison last year. In 2017, a former U.S. Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa. Under a bilateral status of forces agreement, the case is being handled by the Japanese authorities because the suspect was not on duty and was arrested off base.Japanese prosecutors started examining the suspect's case on Monday to determine whether to press formal charges in the coming weeks.
If convicted, he could face life in prison or the death penalty.

sources.headline: Japan summons US envoy as marine arrested over Okinawa murder
sources.text: Ambassador promises cooperation after woman killed on island where bases used by US forces have been long contentious.Japan has summoned the United States ambassador after an American Marine was arrested on suspicion of robbing and killing a woman.US Ambassador to Japan George Glass pledged “full cooperation” on Sunday. Lance-Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard is accused of killing 39-year-old Anna Yagi on the southern island of Okinawa, where thousands of US servicemen are stationed.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Japan denies report Trump told PM Takaichi not to provoke China on Taiwanlist 2 of 3Ex-Japanese Prime Minister Abe’s killer sentenced to lifelist 3 of 3Japan moves to tighten rules for foreigners, throwing futures into doubtend of list“The occurrence of such an extremely brutal and heinous incident is a matter of profound regret,” Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi wrote on social media. “As the Government of Japan, we have lodged a strong protest with the US side, while firmly demanding maximum cooperation with the investigation.”Glass said the US “confirmed our policy of providing full cooperation with the investigation” while sharing his condolences on social media. The 20-year-old Marine has denied the charges.According to local Japanese media, CCTV footage showed a non-Japanese man going into a hotel room with the Japanese woman in the city of Naha. Later on, the footage showed the man leaving by himself with what appears to be the woman’s belongings, the AFP news agency reported.“Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause significant anxiety to the local community and must never occur,” Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi wrote on social media.The Kyodo News agency, quoting police, reported that the woman’s body was found in her hotel room and she appeared to have been strangled.“The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to US bases,” newly elected Okinawa Governor Genta Koja told reporters. “It is absolutely unforgivable, and we are outraged.”“I must say, discipline and troop education are not working at all,” Koja said, referring to the US military’s measures taken in response to past criminal cases.About 54,000 US military personnel, including 18,000 Marines, are stationed in Japan. The majority of these forces are based in Okinawa, a Japanese island that came under US administrative control at the end of World War II and was returned to Japan in 1972.Since the handover, about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested in Japan, according to the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper.The Futenma base, which is located in a densely populated area in central Okinawa, has been a sore spot for decades for locals who have demanded that it be moved.The central government approved construction to relocate the base to Henoko on Okinawa’s eastern coast. However, the project has faced delays.Repeated occurrences of sexual crimes and their delayed disclosures have also angered Okinawans.
